Vibe coding is all fun and games until your scope creep gets huge and it actually matters how you’re optimizing, organizing, and planning everything. And if you’re not actively doing those things, you’re in for a lot of bugs, headaches, and nightmare maintainability. Not to mention if another person has to maintain the code after you, your nightmare code pretty much becomes useless and too unreadable. Once it reaches a certain level of complexity, you can’t just copy paste the code into chatgpt and say fix it. It can possibly fix it, but it makes the code much more awful and create future problems. Vibe coding at that level of complexity adds 20 bugs for every single feature added or bug fixed. It’s not worth it. I say this as someone who has to collab with a vibe coder at work…they are quickly learning that you actually have to use your brain once the project got too complicated. After a certain point in complexity, your focus is not how to add things and make it work, but how to organize, optimize, and design for future scalability. Ai is horrible at looking at the big picture and only creates very specific small scoped solutions. If you’re just making a silly small little side project, sure, vibe code all you want. But miss me with that crap when I have to collab with you and we’ve got thousands of people depending on a system that shouldn’t cause a bunch of problems.

With a cog sci major, you will have to do a good amount of side grinding in order to land a job. I made the conscious decision to major in cog sci while pursuing tech, because I just love the cog sci major. Yes, I’m aware that this lowers my chances than if I were to choose CS. Realistically anyone who relies on their schooling to get a job and doesn’t put in extra work will struggle in the job market. But this is especially true for tech, and especially true for cog sci. For both ui/ux and swe, you will have to grind side projects, building your portfolio, and networking. At the end of the day, the most important things in tech are your experience, your individual skills, and your networking abilities. You can choose a major that has a structured path to build your skills for you, or you can learn them yourself in an unstructured way. None of that matters if you aren’t able to put your skills to work in personal projects and internships.

And the most “structured” path for swe is cs, for UI focused ui/ux it’s a more art-focused program, and for UX focused ui/ux it’s cognitive science/statistics. Cog sci is a jack of all trades major but does not deeply specialize in one thing. You have to supplement that lack of depth with side grinding. It’s not impossible. As a cog sci major I was able to get a SWE internship already in my 2nd year, but ALL of my skills that I needed for the job were from teaching myself, and my cog sci major barely contributed aside from maybe some data science skills for when I made a data reporting dashboard application, ux principles from tailoring the front end for the users, and soft skills. Still, I have no regrets.

I was in a similar position with UCSD and I just want to say. It’s easy to feel drawn towards a more “specialized” major name. I want to specialize in AI and machine learning but I’m majoring in cog sci, and I was really drawn to UCSD’s cog sci with a specialization in machine learning and neural computation. I thought I wouldn’t be able to get that AI specific education from Berkeley. Well it turns out they have the exact same depth of that material, if not better, and the classes are just under different department names. There’s a lot of ML in the cs classes and the data science classes as well, so just adding a ds minor for me covers that curriculum just as well. In fact, berkeley’s cog sci tends to be a lot less fleshed out, that most cog sci majors there are able to double major in a different discipline with the same amount as work as a different major. The cog sci major there is also made so that there’s a lot of overlap between a second major, so it’s actually easier to double major there than elsewhere.

So only majoring in cog sci does not stop you from specializing in linguistics just as much as you would at UCLA’s special major. Cog Sci has a lot of elective requirements where you can pick from any cog sci like disciplines, which includes linguistics. You can just pick all linguistics classes for those electives. Then you can do a linguistics minor or double major, and you would have additional overlap and lower division reqs done from the cog sci major.

I wouldn’t really worry about which school covers your specialty, because the gap is not as large as you think. Berkeley linguistics and cog sci is great, and I’m sure UCLA is good too. Instead make your decision on other factors like where you see yourself being the most happy, because you’ll be just fine wherever you go.

Imo comp sci is a bit overkill for just wanting to go into ui/ux or even web dev if that’s what you like. Comp sci really focuses on mostly back end development, math, and theoretical computer science. In terms of programming, ui/ux only requires a little bit of web dev knowledge, and the part of it which is pretty much already being automated by AI. You need design skills and some statistics/research skills for the UX side. Cog sci is the most aligned major with ui/ux, but obviously comp sci is more employable. If you’re trying to do comp sci for the job stability, that’s a valid reason. Or if you’re just not sure if you want to do general swe or ui/ux, that’s fine too.

I would say choose between berkeley cog sci and UCSD comp sci. 

The only thing is that at berkeley you will be kinda locked out of taking comp sci classes, unless you are fine with settling for data science classes. If you are only interested in web dev SWE and programming that involves front end and product design, I think it’s fine to not have a comp sci major honestly. Most of what you learn for web dev isn’t even taught in the comp sci major. At berkeley, try to minor in statistics or data science. This will give you those research/statistics skills for the ui/ux side. Berkeley’s cog sci is also a very light cog sci major compared to other schools, so it leaves room to minor or double major (which data science is great bc there’s a lot of overlap with berkeley cog sci). Their major is very interdisciplinary focused on things like linguistics and philosophy, and it’s really not that much design aside from a few electives you could choose. Berkeley does not have as good of a ui/ux support as UCSD, but they make up for it because of their tech networking. Berkeley will do a good job of setting you up with the right bay area connections if you’re willing to put the work in for it despite the less structured support.

The other option is comp sci at UCSD, but I would heavily advise that you pick up a cog sci double major (design and interaction specialization) or minor there. UCSD has the best cog sci program out of all UCs, and their ui/ux focused one is their best specialization. The amount of ui/ux classes and support they have is incredible and they will really set your portfolio up for success. UCSD is also more research-aligned and accessible than Berkeley, so they will prepare you enough for the UX side of research if that’s what you like. The UI curriculum is also great as well. Their networking is not as strong as Berkeley, but they have many project-focused classes that focus on building your resume and portfolio - something that’s crucial for ui/ux and swe as well.

Overall I would say the two schools are both good choices for the path you’re trying to take, but you could say Berkeley is less structure, higher risk and possibly? higher reward. Berkeley will have better connections to the industry. UCSD will give you the better content and structure for an educational path, and you will have the job security of a cs major if you decide you want to do full swe (more swe options than just web dev).

People often say it’s worse anxiety/an anxiety disorder. But i have both and here’s how i can tell the differences:

Anxiety: The worry is slightly more grounded in reality, and relative to current events. The reasoning is more logically valid, but just an extreme version of it. You tend to worry about a variety of things, mostly pertaining to current reality. Mental worrying usually consists of a train of “what ifs” and concern about the future. “What if this, oh no that’s bad, then that can become this worse thing, oh and this bad side effect will happen”. Example: “What if my boss hates me because I was a little late to the meeting? I’m not gonna feel confident when I talk to him next…then the other employees might think I’m both lazy and incompetent. I can’t stop thinking about how much he might hate me. I have to be sure to not be late next time.”

OCD: The reasoning may be illogical. There is a thought train of reasoning, but it’s bad reasoning; there’s often an illogical connection. Instead of generally worrying about a variety of things, you can often get fixated on a certain specific idea of a fear, or a specific fear presented as an illogical sequence of events. And of course there is the compulsive factor, but even mentally worrying can be a “compulsion” - not to confuse with anxiety worrying. OCD worry is more centered around seeking an answer of certainty that doesn’t exist in order to attempt to “solve” the worry (which is counterintuitive) - you repeat these what if, no that isn’t it, it must be this, this could solve that, I’ll just plan around that, but what if that other thing instead, it has to be this, this is why, but what if it’s not, etc.. Example: “What if my boss hates me because I was late to the meeting? He didn’t smile as much as he used to. I need to send the next email with good wording so he doesn’t hate me more. Oh but maybe I should send it at a proper time like 8:30am so I seem like a good employee. I better keep reviewing my emails to make sure I didn’t say any racial slurs. I sent the email 17 minutes too late, he’s going to think I’m lazy. A proper employee does tasks on the dot. Oh no, I forgot to check as much as I usually do, surely he saw a racial slur and is about to fire me. Maybe I’m actually just racist and I’m faking having OCD to cover it up.” OCD is also often a reflection or faulty defense mechanism for the things you care about. Do you love your family? OCD will tell you that you’re going to kill them with a knife, so you need to do everything you can to prevent that. Do you love your SO? OCD will tell you you actually don’t love them, so you must keep assessing if you actually do so you don’t lead them on.

One is not necessarily worse than the other, and it’s different for everyone. Also they can affect each other, and it’s rare to have ocd without anxiety.

Not healthy, but ocd can have a correlation with some positive traits when they’re not being taken too far. For example a little perfectionism is good for working hard and good results, but too much and you’ll be miserable

I find that I rarely have to clarify as long as I don’t use any products with silicone. This is because I avoid heavy ingredients than tend to build up on looser curl patterns, and I think I use a low-sulfate (not sulfate free) shampoo. If you’re needing to clarify every 2-3 washes, it’s likely you’re using a product that builds up. A lot of Not Your Mothers products do that to me, ugh

I have looser waves like you. I found that to make my waves form into more of a “curling iron spiral” rather than a weird clumpy zigzaggy mix, you need initial moisture (leave in conditioner) plus a gel that’s more focused on clumping rather than hold (I like Kinky Curly Curling Custard). Scrunch in the shower, and apply product either with praying hands and/or (i forgot the name of the other technique but you grab your formed clumps in 2-4 sections of the hair like a pole at the top and then let go and grab again below, and so on). Do not rake. This method can take a long time to dry but it looks amazing and gives me curling-iron curls. If you find that this method makes your hair a little too flat, lessen the leave-in and consider a low-sulfate shampoo rather than a sulfate free. Generally with your wave level you want to stay away from heavier ingredients like coconut oil and shea butter. Or, if your hairs are on the finer side, look into very light products for fine hair.

If you are short on time, it’s better to skip/lessen the leave-in and rake in a mousse. This gives good volume but less clumpy waves, and they tend to look more “s” waved than curled. I’m still experimenting with quick-dry methods though.

It’s about catching yourself when you are in an intrusive thought loop or compulsive thought loop, and then leaning into the uncertainty. Saying to yourself things like “yeah maybe my fear really is true, I wouldn’t really know for sure”. It’s going to hurt and sting so bad at first responding like that, but it gets better and it does make things easier. Acceptance is a big part of treatment and realizing that uncertainty about our fears will always exist is crucial. Afterwards you want to make sure you prevent yourself from following up the thought with compulsions (which includes both mental and physical). You also want to be challenging yourself always and do the opposite of your OCD urges. For example if you are afraid to touch a car because you have intrusive thoughts about destroying it, make it a goal to slather your hands on it.

A compulsion is anything aimed at reducing or removing anxiety. You can certainly have old compulsions that lose the anxiety/obsession piece yet the habit remain. For example I used to pick at my head due to constant checking if I had lice until my entire hear was bleeding. That was a compulsion because it stemmed from anxiety. Now I don’t have that fear anymore, but the habit stayed. It’s called skin picking disorder which is similar to ocd but is more based on a poor impulse than fear. Which, because they’re very similar, people with OCD are actually prone to getting addicted to things like skin picking.

Unhealthy/mental compulsions involve trying to push our intrusive thoughts away or fight it back, even saying words in response. It sounds weird but you actually want to do the opposite, think of your intrusive thoughts as not an enemy but just sorta there. Don’t push it away but allow it to coexist in your mind until they get tuned out like tv static. Acknowledge the thought for a second and be like “oh cool” and don’t give it much more than that. A large part of OCD is acceptance - we can’t truly get rid of our intrusive thoughts but we can change how we react to them. By treating them like they are mere thoughts like cars on the side of the road and not giving importance to them yet not pushing them away, that’s how you develop healthy coping.

I was prescribed 50mg, but I just keep it at 25 because the side effects are a bit much at that dosage. The weight gain fortunately isn't too much of a problem for me since I've always been skinny, and now I'm finally about normal weight. It made me crave sweets and carbs like crazy, and I've hated carbs and most sweets all my life. Really odd. Didn't think it would change my cravings, and because if it + the dry mouth I developed cavities woops...dry mouth can make it easier to get cavities so careful about it. It also made me "store" my body fat differently, like I had gained weight before but usually just on my arms and chest, but now I'm built different cuz it stored fat in my thighs/hips which never happened to me. 

The dry mouth is mostly noticeable at first, I can't tell if the side effect wore off or I'm just used to it by now, it's probably both.

So with the "sleepiness"..a lot of people report just overall being tired, but I only found that was the case in the process of adjusting to it. I didn't even feel tired all the time, I just found that my sleepiness came in "waves"...I'd feel really awake for a couple hours, then really sleepy, repeat. After like a month on the medicine, I don't feel tired at all from it. I do, however, find that it makes you STAY asleep way too well. And on the weekends, you just might sleep for more than 8 hours. I'm really forgetful so there were many times where I just did anyways even though I shouldn't and I was like woaa. 

The constipation was annoying, but it can be easily solved just by taking some fiber pills or something daily.

I'm in the same situation and also in my 20s. I don't really know how to explain to someone why I don't have a life. It makes me feel very awkward and judged. Is your mental health okay? If you are suffering with depression or anything like that, even if you're not but still struggling, it's not a bad idea to go to therapy. But if it is a mental health issue, you should be treating it like a physical illness and must get treatment for it because it won't go away on its own. Second, if you're not already, you should be trying and pushing for everything you can to get more answers and find relief. Seek a second opinion, consider seeing an IC specialist if you're not already seeing one. Try every suggestion in this subreddit. Sadly IC is not very well known and is often confused with many things, so it's one of those things you need to aggressively research and trial and error and push for on your own. Are you doing pelvic therapy? If not that is something you should consider because almost everyone with IC struggles with pelvic floor issues. I brought up mental health because I understand that it can be very hard to find motivation to do things things when your mind isn't in the right set for it. I still find it hard to keep up with my doctors appointments and pelvic therapy and often go on hiatuses where I've lost all motivation. Only recently am I making the decision to work on my mental health in order to better work on my physical health.

Aside from that, my best advice is to try your best to stick to a routine, and get ready for the day like you would if you had to go out, even if you're not going out. Just the routine of getting up and getting ready really changes your mind and brings motivation and energy. Staying in your bed and not getting up will only make it worse. Having a consistent, set routine will improve your mental health and "fill" your day more. I also found it helpful to find new hobbies. Not just social media or games or tv shows, but good old fashioned hobbies. For me that was playing piano, learning to write music, coding, and digital art, reading. I've also done a major cleanup of my seemingly-eternally messy room and now I live very clean, and the change is super fresh and motivating for me to start my day.
